messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Musician
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 44

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
  Negative Appraisals: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mateo is a 35-year-old married Latino man who makes his living as a musician, and when he speaks about the accident that split his life into a before and after, he does so in a way that is both vivid and strangely incomplete. He had been traveling home after a late-night performance when the life-threatening crash happened. What he can say clearly is that there was a violent impact, the sensation that everything turned without warning, and the conviction in those seconds that he might die. The rest comes to him in jagged fragments rather than a continuous story: a burst of noise, a glimpse of shattered glass, a body pinned at an angle, someone shouting, a flash of light. When he tries to sit still and deliberately remember the sequence, he becomes frustrated and confused. He says it is like reaching for a song he once knew by heart and finding only disconnected bars of melody. He is left with an incomplete picture and the unnerving sense that the worst parts may be hidden somewhere just out of reach.

In the first weeks afterward, Mateo discovered that being by himself was intolerable. Silence left too much room for the broken pieces of the accident to press in. He began filling every open hour with other people. If he was not rehearsing, he was calling friends, meeting other musicians after gigs, lingering at family gatherings, or finding reasons to be in crowded places. He told himself he was staying connected, but privately he knew the real purpose was to make sure he was never alone with his thoughts. The moments he dreaded most were the ones after everyone had gone home, when his mind might turn toward the crash and toward all he could not fully remember.

His marriage gradually took on the strain of that pattern. His wife tried at first to ask what he remembered and how he was feeling, but Mateo would shut the conversation down quickly or leave the room. He did not want to talk about the accident itself, and he did not want to talk about what had changed since. When she asked gently about the aftermath—about his fear, his sleep, the way he seemed unable to tolerate a quiet evening together—he gave short answers or said there was nothing to say. It was not only that the subject upset him; he felt that putting words to it might force him closer to something he was working hard not to think about. Over time, she came to experience him as physically present but emotionally unavailable, especially in the rare quiet hours when they were home together and he would immediately text friends, invite people over, or suggest going out.

His work as a musician gave him a socially acceptable way to remain constantly surrounded. Rehearsals, performances, studio sessions, and late nights with other performers allowed him to stay in motion and in company. He began taking on social invitations he would once have declined, lingering after sets long after he was tired, and arranging jam sessions on days he might otherwise have been home. In the music world, being communal and always around people looked normal from the outside. But Mateo knew he was using the constant presence of others as a shield. The idea of an empty afternoon alone at home felt dangerous to him, as though the missing pieces of the accident might rush in if he gave them space.

Alongside this, his view of himself and his future hardened. He had come to believe that what happened to him was profoundly unfair, and that nothing meaningful had been done about it. That sense of injustice stayed alive in him as a hot, unresolved fact. At the same time, what frightened him most was his own anger. He was certain that if he let himself get too close to it—if he allowed himself to think fully about the accident, or talk openly about how much had been taken from him—he might lose control and do something terrible. He monitored himself for signs of rising rage and often chose company over solitude partly because being with others seemed safer than being alone with the intensity he carried. Beneath all of this was a bleak conclusion that his life had been destroyed by the accident. Even when he was onstage, doing the work that had once made him feel most like himself, there was a sense that he was only occupying the shell of the life he used to have.

By the time he sought help, Mateo was exhausted by the effort it took to stay constantly accompanied and emotionally defended. The immediate push came after his wife told him she no longer recognized the man she was living with: someone always busy, always out, always changing the subject whenever anything real came close. He came to treatment not because he was ready to tell the whole story—he still found that impossible—but because he was scared of what might happen if he kept living this way. He was afraid that if his anger ever broke through, he would not be able to control it, and equally afraid that if he stopped outrunning his thoughts, he would have to face a life he already believed had been ruined. What he hopes for, though he says it cautiously, is to be able to be alone without panic, to speak to his wife without shutting down, and to understand what happened to him well enough that it no longer feels like a shattered piece of his life lodged permanently inside him.
